title: How are sealed classes and records complementary in Java's pattern-matching vision?
shortTitle: How are sealed classes and records complementary in Java's pattern-matching vision?
keyPoints: Sealed types say "it is exactly one of these" (sum type); records say "and here are its fields" (product type).
Pattern matching in `switch` reads both in a single exhaustive step.
Record patterns deconstruct a record's components directly in a case: `case Transfer(var from, var to, var amount)`.
Records are implicitly `final`, so they satisfy the sealed-subtype rule automatically.
Guarded patterns (`when` clause) layer business conditions on top of structural matching.
Adding a new permitted record type fails every exhaustive switch at compile time.
Nested record patterns destructure records inside records in a single expression.

s1_definition.oneliner: Sealed types say "it is exactly one of these," records say "and here are its fields," and pattern matching reads both in a single exhaustive switch.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Sealed type = sum** – defines a closed set of permitted subtypes; a value is exactly one of the alternatives.
- **Record = product** – defines an immutable, transparent bundle of named components; a value bundles fields.
- **Record pattern** – destructures a record's components directly in a `case`: `case Transfer(var from, var to, var amount)`.
- **Exhaustive switch** – over a sealed type, the compiler verifies every permitted case is handled without a `default`.
- **Guarded pattern** – refines a case with a `when` condition for business logic.
- **Implicit final** – records satisfy the `final`/`sealed`/`non-sealed` rule automatically.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has a fixed menu of exactly three transaction types: Deposit, Withdrawal, and Transfer. That closed menu is the sealed type. Each transaction type is a pre-printed form with fixed fields: a Transfer form always has "from account", "to account", and "amount." That fixed form is the record. When a clerk processes a transaction, they first look at which form it is (sealed choice) and then immediately read the fields printed on it (record deconstruction).

sections.s3_flow:
```text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Sealed + Records + Pattern Matching        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                             │
│  sealed interface Txn (SUM TYPE)            │
│       │                                     │
│       ├── record Deposit(acct, amt)  PRODUCT│
│       ├── record Withdrawal(acct, amt) PROD │
│       └── record Transfer(from, to, amt) PR │
│                                             │
│  switch (txn):                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐       │
│  │ case Deposit(var a, var amt)     │       │
│  │   → use a, amt directly         │       │
│  │                                  │       │
│  │ case Withdrawal(var a, var amt)  │       │
│  │   → use a, amt directly         │       │
│  │                                  │       │
│  │ case Transfer(var f, var t, amt) │       │
│  │   when amt > LIMIT              │       │
│  │   → flag as high value          │       │
│  │                                  │       │
│  │ case Transfer(var f, var t, amt) │       │
│  │   → normal transfer             │       │
│  └──────────────────────────────────┘       │
│  Exhaustive: no default needed ✓            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Sealed classes and records are the two halves of algebraic data types in Java. A sealed type is a sum type that says a value is exactly one of a closed set of alternatives. A record is a product type that bundles named components into an immutable value. Pattern matching consumes both in a single exhaustive switch.

In a banking system at National Bank of India, Pankaj models transactions as a sealed `Txn` interface permitting three records: `Deposit`, `Withdrawal`, and `Transfer`. The processor uses record patterns to bind components directly in each case, and a guarded case flags high-value transfers for compliance review. No `default` branch is needed because the compiler knows the set is complete.

The real payoff is safety. If the bank introduces a fourth transaction kind, every exhaustive switch across the codebase fails to compile until it handles the new kind. That turns "we forgot to handle a case" from a production incident into a compile error. At the same time, record patterns keep the processing code clean because you read the structure declaratively without chains of getter calls.

The senior point is to avoid `default` over a sealed type because a `default` would silently swallow a newly added subtype. Records are implicitly `final`, so they satisfy the sealed-subtype rule automatically. Guarded patterns with `when` layer business conditions without breaking exhaustiveness, and nested record patterns destructure inner records in one expression.

Remember one sentence: sealed types describe which alternatives exist, records describe the fields inside each alternative, and pattern matching consumes both at once with compiler-checked exhaustiveness.
